parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what stays the same and what keeps changing when an object goes round a circle at steady rate - consider speed versus velocity as a vector.
Hint 2: Think about which way the acceleration must point to keep bending the velocity vector, and how its size and its angle to velocity behave.
parts.proper_answer: Speed is constant so velocity has constant magnitude but its direction changes continuously, always tangential to the circle. Acceleration has constant magnitude, directed towards the centre, perpendicular to velocity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Velocity in uniform circular motion**
Uniform means the rate of going round is steady, so the speed is constant. But velocity is a vector. Its direction is always along the tangent to the circle and it keeps rotating as the object moves, so velocity is constantly changing even though its magnitude is constant.

Step 2: **Acceleration in uniform circular motion**
Because velocity direction changes, there must be an acceleration. This is the centripetal acceleration, always directed towards the centre of the circle. Its magnitude is constant, and because a tangent is always at 90 degrees to a radius, the acceleration is always perpendicular to the velocity: $$a = \frac{v^2}{R} \text{ towards centre}$$

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Recall how arc length travelled in one revolution links linear distance to angle, and think how speed relates to angular speed for radius R.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Linking linear and angular speed**
In time $t$ the angle swept is $\theta = \omega t$ and the arc distance travelled is $s = R\theta$. Speed is distance over time, so $$v = \frac{s}{t} = \frac{R\theta}{t} = R\omega$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Start from a standard form for centripetal acceleration that uses R and omega, or R and v.
Hint 2: Use your result $v = R\omega$ to eliminate R and leave only $v$ and $\omega$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Standard centripetal form**
The magnitude of centripetal acceleration can be written as: $$a = R\omega^2$$ which is the same as $$a = \frac{v^2}{R}$$

Step 2: **Eliminate R**
From (b)(i), $R = v/\omega$. Substituting into $a = R\omega^2$ gives: $$a = \left(\frac{v}{\omega}\right)\omega^2 = v\omega$$

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at triangle OBP in Fig. 1.1 - OP is one side, the line from the ball to the screen is parallel to OP, and OB is the hypotenuse R. Which trig ratio links x to angle theta?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Right triangle geometry**
Point P is directly above O, and the shadow is directly above B because the light rays are parallel. So $x$ is the side opposite angle $\theta$ in a right triangle with hypotenuse $OB = R$. Hence: $$\sin\theta = \frac{x}{R}$$ so $$x = R\sin\theta$$

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Remember the definition of angular speed as rate of change of angle, and use the condition that theta starts at zero.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Angle grows steadily with time**
Angular speed is defined by $\omega = \Delta\theta / \Delta t$. With $\theta = 0$ at $t = 0$ and constant $\omega$, the angle swept in time $t$ is simply: $$\theta = \omega t$$

parts.label: (c)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Take your geometric result for x in terms of theta and replace theta with your time-dependent expression.
parts.proper_answer: Substituting $\theta = \omega t$ into $x = R\sin\theta$ gives $x = R\sin\omega t$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Combine geometry and rotation**
From (c)(i) $$x = R\sin\theta$$ and from (c)(ii) $$\theta = \omega t$$ Direct substitution of $\theta$ gives: $$x = R\sin\omega t$$ This shows displacement of the shadow varies sinusoidally with time.

parts.label: (c)(iv)
hints: Hint 1: Compare $x = R\sin\omega t$ with the standard mathematical form for SHM displacement starting at zero.
parts.proper_answer: $x = R\sin\omega t$ is of the form $x = x_0\sin\omega t$ with constant amplitude $R$, which defines simple harmonic motion.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recognising SHM form**
Simple harmonic motion is defined by a sinusoidal displacement-time relation such as $$x = x_0\sin\omega t$$ Here $x = R\sin\omega t$ has exactly that form, with $x_0 = R$ constant and $\omega$ constant. So the projection - the shadow - executes SHM.

parts.label: (d)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about how far the shadow can move from the centre P - what is the largest possible value of x in $x = R\sin\omega t$?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Amplitude equals radius**
Maximum of $\sin\omega t$ is 1, so maximum $x$ is $R$. The diameter is $0.46\text{ m}$, so: $$x_0 = R = \frac{0.46}{2} = 0.23\text{ m}$$

parts.label: (d)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall the link between angular speed omega and time for one full oscillation, involving $2\pi$ radians.
Hint 2: Rearrange to make period T the subject and insert $\omega = 1.9\text{ rad s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Omega-period relation**
One oscillation corresponds to $2\pi$ rad, so: $$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$$

Step 2: **Calculate T**
Rearranging: $$T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi}{1.9} = 3.3\text{ s}$$ The shadow takes the same time as one revolution of the ball.

parts.label: (d)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall the SHM rule for acceleration magnitude $a = \omega^2 x$, and think where it is largest.
Hint 2: Insert $\omega = 1.9\text{ rad s}^{-1}$ and your amplitude $0.23\text{ m}$ to find the maximum value.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Maximum acceleration formula**
In SHM, acceleration is greatest at maximum displacement: $$a_0 = \omega^2 x_0$$

parts.label: (e)
hints: Hint 1: Remember acceleration in SHM always points back to equilibrium, $a = -\omega^2 x$, so think what sign of x gives positive (to the right) acceleration.
parts.proper_answer: Mark A at maximum negative displacement, i.e. on the screen to the left of P, above the left-hand edge of the circular path.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Where is acceleration most positive?**
Take positive $x$ to the right as in Fig. 1.1. In SHM $$a = -\omega^2 x$$ so acceleration is positive when $x$ is negative. Maximum positive $a$ occurs at maximum negative $x$, i.e. $x = -R$. That is the leftmost extreme of the shadow motion, on the screen directly above the left side of the ball's circular path. Label this point A.
